p.title: Similarity-based link prediction in social networks using latent relationships between the users

ext.title: Similarity-based link prediction in social networks using latent relationships between the users
ext.document_type: Journal article, open access (CC BY 4.0), 11 pages
ext.coverage: Full text read in chunks, from title page through the author-contributions and licence page (text file 41,391 chars, 841 lines). Metadata hint is correct; no correction needed. All 38 items in the annotation file (_annots/a6421bb84f3f.json) were read. Every item is a Highlight by Paul Goff, with no sticky notes, typed comments or note text. Highlight colours: 1 green (0.49, 0.78, 0.41) and 37 yellow (0.98, 0.80, 0.35). Several highlights overlap and their covered text is interleaved, so fragments are marked [...]. Topic check: the paper covers networks, path-based (semi-local) similarity indices and link prediction. It contains no content on lobbying, allocation, elections, persuasion or turnout, legislators, or text measurement.
ext.research_question: Can similarity scores for link prediction that go beyond common first-order neighbours (through a latent relationship captured by the correlation of second-order neighbourhood profiles) predict missing or future links more accurately than eight established similarity baselines?
ext.theory: No named social theory. The premise is that structural similarity between two nodes predicts link formation (pp.1-2, citing Ke-ke et al. / Shang et al., ref 18). Common neighbours are treated as an incomplete measure, and a latent relationship is defined as indirect connectivity through second-order neighbours (p.2). Hypothesis 1: if two nodes with a future link have no common neighbour but a significant latent relationship, the link can be predicted. Hypothesis 2: latent relationships separate existing from non-existing links even when pairs share the same number of common neighbours (p.4).
ext.data: Nine static real-world networks, each treated as one snapshot with no time dimension (Table 1, p.8): KRT Zachary karate club (34 nodes, 78 edges, social); DLN dolphins (62, 159, animal); UAL US airline traffic (332, 2126, airport traffic); NSC NetScience co-authorship (379, 914); INF face-to-face contacts at an exhibition (410, 2765); EML Rovira i Virgili email (1133, 5451); YST yeast biological network (2284, 6646); HAM Hamsterster social network (2426, 16630); KHN co-authorship (3772, 12718). Unit of analysis: node pairs (existing edges and non-existing pairs). No collection period is stated. Each network's sample is the full network as published, with no sampling step described.
ext.method: Similarity-based link prediction. For each node i, a neighbourhood vector N_i (Eq. 10, p.6) has entries d_i at the node itself, CN_iz for second-order neighbours, CN_iz + 1 for first-order neighbours, and 0 otherwise. The union set UN_ij (Eq. 11) is the set of indices where either vector is positive. The indirect similarity Corr_ij is the Pearson correlation of N_i and N_j over UN_ij (Eqs. 12-13). The DICN score is DICN_ij = (1 + CN_ij)(1 + Corr_ij) (Eq. 14, p.7). Algorithm 1 (p.6) gives the pseudo-code. Evaluation: edges are randomly split into a training set (beta = 80% by default, 50-90% swept in Exp. 2) and a test set; the process is repeated 15 times and averaged. AUC (Eq. 15, pp.7-8) is computed by comparing every test edge with every non-existing pair, counting ties as 0.5. Eight baselines were implemented in Java: CN, PA, JC, HPI, CNDP, NCC, CCPA and SHOPI.
ext.identification: None in the causal sense. The design is out-of-sample link prediction using random edge holdout. Hypotheses 1 and 2 are tested by restricting test and non-existing pairs to subsets defined by common-neighbour status (Exp. 3 and Exp. 4, pp.9-10).
ext.scope: Population: nine public real-world networks of mixed type (social, animal, airline, co-authorship, contact, biological, email), all treated as static. The paper does not claim a broader population. Era: not stated; published 2020. The paper names directed and weighted networks as future work (p.10), which implies none were analysed.

key_findings.finding: Common neighbours miss many links: a share of existing edges have no common neighbour. Shares range from 3.1% (UAL) to 53.7% (YST).

Existing and non-existing links overlap heavily at the same common-neighbour count, so the count alone separates them poorly. Fig. 2 shows the overlap, with roughly an even split near 8 common neighbours for INF, EML and YST.
key_findings.numbers: around 8 common neighbours (INF, EML, YST); no tabulated values in the text

key_findings.finding: Proposed DICN score combines direct similarity (common neighbours) with indirect similarity (Pearson correlation of second-order neighbourhood vectors). Worked examples: Corr_25 about -0.74 gives DICN_25 = 0.26; Corr_38 about 0.32 and Corr_31 about 0.01 for the Fig. 3 pairs.
key_findings.numbers: DICN_25 = 0.26; Corr_25 about -0.74; Corr_38 about 0.32; Corr_31 about 0.01

key_findings.finding: Experiment 1 (beta = 80): DICN has the highest AUC in eight of nine networks. In UAL it is close to the best but not the best.
key_findings.numbers: DICN vs best other: KRT 0.7654 vs 0.7336 (CNDP); DLN 0.7943 vs 0.7570 (CCPA); UAL 0.9367 vs 0.9416 (NCC); NSC 0.9747 vs 0.9195 (CNDP); INF 0.9553 vs 0.9483 (CCPA); EML 0.8932 vs 0.8729 (SHOPI); YST 0.8278 vs 0.7892 (CCPA); HAM 0.9725 vs 0.9617 (CCPA); KHN 0.8839 vs 0.8509 (SHOPI)

key_findings.finding: Experiment 2 (beta swept 50-90): DICN is consistently best for beta of 70 or higher in seven of nine networks. It is not always best at small training fractions, which the authors attribute to weaker detectable correlation.
key_findings.numbers: seven of nine networks at beta >= 70; Fig. 5 values not given in text

key_findings.finding: Experiment 3 (Hypothesis 1, pairs with no common neighbours and degree > 1): among PA, CCPA, SHOPI and DICN, DICN is best in five networks and close to the best in the other four.
key_findings.numbers: DICN best: KRT 0.8319, NSC 0.8471, EML 0.7595, HAM 0.7831, KHN 0.8001. Others: DLN 0.7028 vs CCPA 0.7211; UAL 0.7979 vs SHOPI 0.8091; INF 0.7979 vs SHOPI 0.8404; YST 0.7609 vs PA 0.7755

key_findings.finding: Experiment 4 (Hypothesis 2, pairs with equal common-neighbour counts; compared with NCC, CNDP, CCPA, SHOPI): DICN is best in five networks, near the best in three, and clearly worst in UAL.
key_findings.numbers: DICN best: NSC 0.7815, INF 0.7712, EML 0.7495, HAM 0.7483, KHN 0.7829. Near best: KRT 0.6728 vs SHOPI 0.6919; DLN 0.6508 vs CCPA 0.6510; YST 0.7595 vs CCPA 0.7613. UAL: DICN 0.5684 vs SHOPI 0.7921

key_findings.finding: AUC worked example: with five non-existing edges and one test edge (DICN_35 = 2.5), n1 = 3 and n2 = 1 give AUC = 0.7. The AUC formula is (n1 + n2/2)/n.
Motivating example: CN gives S_24 = 1 > S_45 = 0, yet nodes 4 and 5 may share a latent relationship via their neighbours 2 and 3.

measures: Significance of Higher-Order Path Index (SHOPI, Eqs. 8-9)
DICN (proposed): (1 + CN)(1 + Pearson correlation of neighbourhood vectors), Eq. 14
Neighbourhood vector N_i (Eq. 10) and union neighbourhood set UN_ij (Eq. 11)
limitations: Stated by the authors: when the training set is small, the latent relationship is harder to detect because the correlation is lower, so DICN may be less accurate (p.9).
Stated by the authors: in UAL, and in Exp. 4 more generally, NCC, CNDP and SHOPI significantly outperform DICN (p.10).
Stated by the authors: the latent relationship is restricted to second-order neighbours; extending it to path counts or node centrality is future work (p.10).
Stated by the authors: directed and weighted networks, and more varied networks, are future work (p.10).
Reviewer observation (not stated by the authors): AUC is the only metric. No standard deviation or significance test across the 15 random splits is reported, only averages.
Reviewer observation: the Experiment 3 text calls the four non-DICN-best networks 'very close' to the best, but the INF gap is 0.8404 vs 0.7979 (SHOPI vs DICN).
Reviewer observation: the self-entry d_i is part of the vector and therefore enters the Pearson correlation (Eq. 10). The effect of degree on Corr_ij is not separately examined.
Reviewer observation: the paper gives 8 MB memory for the test machine (p.7). This is probably a typo for GB, but the text reads 8 MB as printed.

rel.summary_md:
Zareie and Sakellariou propose DICN, a link-prediction score that multiplies a direct term (1 + common neighbours) by an indirect term (1 + the Pearson correlation of two nodes' neighbourhood vectors, which include second-order neighbours). They motivate it with two observations. First, between 3.1% (UAL) and 53.7% (YST) of existing edges join nodes that share no common neighbour. Second, at the same common-neighbour count, linked and unlinked pairs overlap heavily. They test it on nine small, static, unweighted, undirected networks, holding out 20% of edges at random over 15 repeats and scoring with AUC only. DICN has the highest AUC in 8 of 9 networks. The margins over the best baseline range from about 0.01 (INF, HAM) to about 0.055 (NSC), and DICN loses on UAL. It also wins in 5 of 9 networks on pairs with no common neighbour, and in 5 of 9 on pairs with equal common-neighbour counts, where it is clearly worst on UAL (0.568 vs 0.792). No variances or significance tests are reported. Weighted and directed graphs are left to future work.

For Melange, the paper is a candidate source of dyadic features, not evidence about influence. The sharpest use is in the ridge-logistic cosponsor forecaster. Its only pair-level network signal is the direct prior sponsor-to-member affinity count. Every other network term describes a single node (degree, eigenvector), so common-neighbour and second-order similarity between the sponsor and the candidate are missing. The press HCoI layer already uses the correlation-of-profiles idea through Malaterre, but it uses correlation alone, without the direct term. Any DICN-style score in this system is a heuristic similarity output, not closeness, access or introduction probability (D-025). It stays UNVERIFIED until it is reproduced under the forecaster's own temporal split (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Common-neighbour plus second-order correlation similarity (DICN) beats eight baselines in AUC in 8 of 9 networks at a beta = 80% training split (e.g. NSC 0.9747 vs 0.9195 CNDP; KHN 0.8839 vs 0.8509 SHOPI; loses on UAL 0.9367 vs 0.9416). On pairs with no common neighbour it is best in 5 of 9 (e.g. KRT 0.8319, NSC 0.8471).
bearings.paper_location: Table 2 p.9 (Exp. 1); Table 3 pp.9-10 (Exp. 3); Eq. 14 p.7
bearings.system_side: The forecaster scores (bill, member) candidates with ridge logistic regression on prior-Congress features. Its only dyadic network feature is the direct prior affinity count/rate between member and sponsor. Degree and eigenvector are member-level. There is no common-neighbour, Jaccard/Adamic-Adar, or second-order similarity feature between the sponsor and the candidate.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper uses random edge holdout on static, unweighted, undirected graphs of 34-3,772 nodes. The forecaster is temporal (Congress t-1 graph predicts Congress t joins), directed (sponsor to cosponsor), bill-level and weighted. Paper gains are about 0.01-0.05 AUC with no variance reported. A sponsor-candidate CN/DICN feature computed on the prior-Congress HR/S graph is a cheap candidate to test against the existing affinity baseline. Any lift must be shown on the forecaster's own temporal split; until then it is UNVERIFIED (DE-062). Pairs with zero prior affinity are where Exp. 3 suggests the most value.

bearings.paper_claim: Indirect similarity (Pearson correlation of neighbourhood vectors) is combined multiplicatively with direct common neighbours rather than used alone, as (1 + CN)(1 + Corr). Correlation-driven scoring underperforms where structure is hub-dominated (UAL, Exp. 4: 0.5684 vs SHOPI 0.7921). With smaller training fractions, correlation becomes hard to detect.
bearings.paper_location: Eqs. 12-14 pp.6-7; Table 4 p.10; Exp. 2 p.9
bearings.system_side: HCoI builds member-member edges purely from Pearson correlation of recency-weighted press-category profiles (threshold 0.6), then runs Louvain (seed 7). It does not combine that with any direct cosponsor tie, and homophily replication at press resolution was null.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The analogy is loose. HCoI correlates topic-attention profiles, not neighbourhood vectors, and the paper never tests correlation alone. The transferable point is design: a profile correlation is one half of the score, and the paper anchors it on direct shared ties. That fits HCoI's documented null if correlation alone is a weak tie signal. Using it only to place cosponsor-isolated members (D4) is consistent with Exp. 3 (no-CN pairs). That use is still a heuristic placement, not evidence of a relationship.

bearings.paper_claim: First-order neighbourhoods miss many real ties: 3.1%-53.7% of existing edges join nodes with no common neighbour. Second-order neighbourhood correlation recovers some of that signal.
bearings.system_side: Neighbour imputation averages stance tiers over direct cosponsor-graph neighbours only, with at least 5 informative neighbours (SD_MINNB) and |estimate| >= 0.75. Members with fewer direct neighbours get no proposal. Masking gives 77% sign agreement; co-movement was null.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper predicts edges, not node attributes, so it supports at most a second-order similarity weight for choosing which neighbours to average. The null co-movement result already limits how much network-based imputation can carry. Treat any second-order variant as a proposal that must beat a party-only baseline on masked cells. Weak.

bearings.paper_claim: Works only with unsigned, unweighted, undirected similarity; it has no treatment of negative or signed ties.
bearings.paper_location: Problem definition p.1; future work p.10
bearings.system_side: Signed, directed member-reference edges carry LLM valence per context window (green above +0.15, red below -0.15), and unsigned co-appearance pairs are display only.
bearings.transfer_conditions: No transfer for the signed layer. The component list cites Zareie & Sakellariou 2020 for this component, but the paper offers nothing on negative ties or valence. At most it could score unsigned co-appearance pairs for missing-link candidates, which is display only.

gaps_exposed: The cosponsor forecaster has no sponsor-candidate structural-similarity feature (common neighbours, Jaccard, Adamic-Adar, or second-order correlation). Its only dyadic network signal is direct prior affinity, so pairs with zero prior history get only node-level and ideology terms.

No link-prediction benchmark exists in the system. The engine kernel, recruitment paths and cascades treat a missing cosponsor tie as p = 0, with no estimate of how many ties are merely unobserved. The paper finds that up to 53.7% of edges lack common neighbours in some networks.

There is no evaluation of any system tie-inference layer (HCoI correlation edges, co-appearance) as a predictor of later cosponsor ties by AUC under a temporal holdout. The paper's evaluation protocol (AUC with ties counted as 0.5, Eq. 15) is a ready template, adapted to temporal rather than random splits.
flags: D-025: any DICN or common-neighbour score added to the system is a heuristic similarity output. It must never be described as closeness, access or introduction probability.

Rejected SNA proposals: the paper argues for neither dropping regular cosponsorship edges nor per-edge volume normalization. However, DICN is defined only on unweighted graphs, so a naive port would binarize the cosponsor graph and erase the 1.0/0.5 original/regular distinction. Do not let a DICN port quietly re-introduce the rejected edge changes; compute it on the existing graph or a documented weighted extension.

Component list mismatch: Zareie & Sakellariou 2020 is listed as a citation for melange-sna.co-appearance-and-references, which concerns negative or signed ties. The paper is unsigned and gives no basis for negative-tie handling.
Paul filed the paper under 'Path-Finding Algorithums'. It is a link-prediction (similarity) paper with no path-finding content.

Evidence quality: the only metric is AUC, averaged over 15 random splits, with no variance or significance tests and static benchmark graphs. Any system use is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
rel.paul_alignment: Paul left no takeaway for this paper. Both bibliography entries are citation-only, and his PDF markup is 38 plain highlights with no notes. The highlights focus on the claim that common neighbours alone are insufficient, the neighbourhood-vector and correlation construction, and the no-common-neighbour experiment. The paper supports that emphasis, but the gains are modest (about 0.01-0.05 AUC) and come from small, static, unweighted benchmarks. Filing it under path-finding understates its real use: it supplies dyadic similarity features for link and cosponsor prediction. The component list also cites it for negative ties in the co-appearance and reference layers, which it does not address. Nothing in his notes is stale against the built system, because the system never adopted this method. The closest built analogue is HCoI's profile correlation, which came from Malaterre, not from this paper.

related.why: Both infer ties from Pearson correlation of profile vectors (Malaterre with topic profiles at a 0.6 threshold, used in press_hcoi.py). Zareie anchors the correlation on direct common neighbours.
Signed link prediction. It covers the negative-tie question the co-appearance and reference layer needs, which Zareie's unsigned similarity cannot answer.
Negative link prediction in social media fills the signed-tie gap that this unsigned common-neighbour method leaves open.
Supplies the weighted, directed cosponsorship graph on which a DICN-style dyadic feature would have to be adapted (Zareie leaves weighted and directed graphs to future work).
Same first author. The 2023 survey covers behaviour-aware influence maximization, the downstream use of similarity and tie estimates in the cascade engines.
